title: Investing
intro: Investing is putting money into something today in the expectation of getting more back later. This topic takes you from the arithmetic of compound interest to the models professionals use to price bonds and options, build portfolios and judge evidence, for every major kind of asset: stocks, bonds, funds, currencies, real estate, commodities and derivatives.

blocks.text: Every investment is a claim on future cash. A share is a claim on a company's future profits; a bond is a promise of fixed payments; a currency deposit earns that country's interest rate; an option is a right whose value depends on where a price ends up. Learning to invest is learning to ask the same questions of each: what cash will it pay, when, how sure is it, and what am I paying for it today?

blocks.alt: A map of the main asset classes arranged by typical risk and expected return: cash and short government bills at the low end, then government bonds, investment-grade corporate bonds, high-yield bonds, real estate, large-company stocks, small-company and emerging-market stocks, and at the far end commodities, options and crypto, which have high risk without a reliable expected return.
blocks.caption: Asset classes placed roughly by their long-run risk and return. The order is typical, not guaranteed: in any given year the ranking can flip.

items: Foundations. The Mathematics of Money (compounding, present value, inflation, the rule of 72) and How Markets and Accounts Work (exchanges, brokers, orders, account types).
Stocks. What owning a share means, how to read financial statements, and how to value a company with multiples and discounted cash flow.
Bonds. Price and yield, duration and convexity, government bonds around the world, corporate credit, and the yield curve and central banks.
Funds. Mutual funds, ETFs, index funds, and why costs matter more than almost anything else you control.

Currencies. How exchange rates are quoted, what the major currencies are used for (the dollar as reserve, the yen and franc as funding and safe havens, the commodity currencies), and the parity conditions and carry trade.
Real assets and alternatives. Real estate and REITs, gold and commodities, private markets and crypto.
Derivatives. Futures, forwards and swaps; then options, their strategies, and the binomial and Black-Scholes models with the Greeks.
Portfolios. Risk and return measured properly, Modern Portfolio Theory, CAPM and factor models, market efficiency, building and rebalancing a real portfolio, and spending from it.
Judgment. Behavioral finance, how to research an investment and read the evidence, and taxes, fees and the classic pitfalls.

blocks.text: This is education, not personal advice. Rules on accounts and taxes differ by country and change over time; where a page uses an example it is usually the United States, and it says so. Check current rules before you act on them.
Ten ideas that carry most of the weight

items: Compounding is the engine. Money growing at 7% a year doubles in about 10 years and grows about 7.6 times in 30. Time in the market matters more than the exact entry point.
Risk and expected return travel together, but only for risk you cannot diversify away. The market pays you for bearing broad economic risk, not for holding one stock that could go to zero.
Diversify. Owning many assets that don't move together cuts risk with little or no cost to expected return. It is the closest thing to a free lunch in finance.
Costs compound too. A 1% yearly fee takes roughly a quarter of the final balance over 30 years. Low-cost index funds beat most active managers after fees.
Price matters. A wonderful company can be a poor investment if you pay too much. Valuation links what you pay to what you get.
Bonds fall when rates rise. A bond's duration tells you by roughly how much.
Leverage cuts both ways and can turn a temporary loss into a permanent one through a margin call.
Inflation is the quiet risk. Cash that earns less than inflation loses buying power every year.
You are your own biggest risk. Selling in a panic, chasing last year's winners and trading too much cost ordinary investors more than any market crash.
Match the investment to the goal. Money needed within about five years should not sit in stocks; money for 30 years from now should not sit in cash.

blocks.text: How to use the tools here

Most pages have a plot you can drive with sliders (compound growth, bond prices, option payoffs, the efficient frontier and more) and practice problems with hidden hints and solutions. Highlight any term to see its glossary definition. The arrows at the foot of each page step through the topic in reading order.
